mechanism: Replenishes hepatic glutathione, detoxifying the reactive metabolite NAPQI and preventing hepatocellular necrosis.
dosing: IV per weight-based protocol (e.g. 21-hour or SNAP regimen); most effective within 8 hours of ingestion but give later if indicated by nomogram/staggered ingestion.

references.label: National poisons information service / TOXBASE; WHO antidote guidance

mechanism: Competitive mu-opioid receptor antagonist, reversing respiratory depression and sedation.
dosing: 0.4-2 mg IV/IM/intranasal, titrated to adequate ventilation; repeat or infuse as needed (short half-life, may need re-dosing).

references.label: National poisons information service / TOXBASE; WHO antidote guidance

mechanism: Competitive antagonist at the benzodiazepine site of the GABA-A receptor.
dosing: 0.2 mg IV repeated cautiously. Use selectively - can precipitate seizures in benzodiazepine-dependent patients or mixed (e.g. TCA) overdose.

references.label: National poisons information service / TOXBASE; WHO antidote guidance

mechanism: Atropine blocks muscarinic effects of acetylcholine excess; pralidoxime reactivates acetylcholinesterase (give with atropine for organophosphates).
dosing: Atropine doubling-dose regimen titrated to drying of secretions/clear chest; add pralidoxime for organophosphates per protocol.

references.label: National poisons information service / TOXBASE; WHO antidote guidance

mechanism: Reactivates acetylcholinesterase by removing the phosphoryl group before 'ageing'; relieves nicotinic (and some muscarinic) effects.
dosing: Give early (before enzyme ageing) alongside atropine, by infusion per protocol.

references.label: National poisons information service / TOXBASE; WHO antidote guidance

mechanism: Chelates free ferric iron to form renally-excreted ferrioxamine.
dosing: IV infusion ~15 mg/kg/hour for severe toxicity (shock, acidosis, high level); watch for hypotension with rapid infusion.

references.label: National poisons information service / TOXBASE; WHO antidote guidance

mechanism: Ovine Fab fragments bind free digoxin, forming inert complexes that are renally excreted.
dosing: Dose by ingested amount or serum level/body weight; give empirically for life-threatening arrhythmia, significant hyperkalaemia or instability.

references.label: National poisons information service / TOXBASE; WHO antidote guidance

mechanism: Inhibits alcohol dehydrogenase, preventing formation of toxic metabolites (formic acid / oxalate); the parent alcohol is then cleared or dialysed.
dosing: IV loading 15 mg/kg then maintenance per protocol; combine with sodium bicarbonate, cofactors and haemodialysis for severe toxicity.

references.label: National poisons information service / TOXBASE; WHO antidote guidance

mechanism: Activates cardiac adenylate cyclase independently of beta-receptors, raising cAMP to improve inotropy and chronotropy.
dosing: Bolus then infusion; combine with high-dose insulin euglycaemia therapy, calcium, vasopressors and pacing for refractory toxicity.

references.label: National poisons information service / TOXBASE; WHO antidote guidance

mechanism: Increases extracellular calcium to overcome channel blockade and support contractility.
dosing: IV calcium boluses/infusion with cardiac monitoring; combine with high-dose insulin euglycaemia therapy, glucagon and vasopressors.

references.label: National poisons information service / TOXBASE; WHO antidote guidance

mechanism: Vitamin K restores synthesis of functional clotting factors II, VII, IX, X; prothrombin complex concentrate replaces them immediately for major bleeding.
dosing: Oral/IV vitamin K guided by INR and bleeding; add four-factor PCC (or FFP) for major haemorrhage.

references.label: National poisons information service / TOXBASE; WHO antidote guidance

mechanism: Positively-charged protamine binds and neutralises negatively-charged heparin.
dosing: IV dose calculated from heparin given/time elapsed; only partially reverses LMWH.

references.label: National poisons information service / TOXBASE; WHO antidote guidance

mechanism: Humanised antibody fragment that binds dabigatran with very high affinity, neutralising its anticoagulant effect.
dosing: 5 g IV (two 2.5 g vials) for life-threatening bleeding or urgent surgery.

references.label: National poisons information service / TOXBASE; WHO antidote guidance

mechanism: Provides a circulating 'lipid sink' that sequesters lipophilic local anaesthetic and supports cardiac energetics.
dosing: 1.5 mL/kg 20% bolus then infusion, repeated for persistent collapse, alongside standard resuscitation.

references.label: National poisons information service / TOXBASE; WHO antidote guidance

mechanism: Binds cyanide to form renally-excreted cyanocobalamin (vitamin B12).
dosing: 5 g IV (repeat to 10 g) for suspected significant cyanide toxicity.

references.label: National poisons information service / TOXBASE; WHO antidote guidance

mechanism: Acts as an electron carrier (via NADPH-methaemoglobin reductase) to reduce methaemoglobin back to haemoglobin.
dosing: 1-2 mg/kg IV over 5 minutes; avoid/caution in G6PD deficiency (may cause haemolysis and be ineffective).

references.label: National poisons information service / TOXBASE; WHO antidote guidance

mechanism: Suppresses pancreatic insulin secretion, preventing recurrent hypoglycaemia after dextrose correction.
dosing: SC/IV octreotide for refractory or recurrent sulfonylurea hypoglycaemia, alongside dextrose.

references.label: National poisons information service / TOXBASE; WHO antidote guidance

mechanism: Antibodies neutralise circulating venom toxins.
dosing: Give for systemic envenomation/coagulopathy/neurotoxicity per local protocol; have adrenaline ready for reactions.

references.label: National poisons information service / TOXBASE; WHO antidote guidance

mechanism: Bypasses dihydrofolate reductase inhibition by providing reduced folate (5-formyl-tetrahydrofolate), rescuing normal cells from methotrexate-induced one-carbon block.
dosing: Standard rescue: folinic acid 15 mg PO/IV every 6 hours starting 24h after high-dose MTX, continued until MTX level <0.05 micromol/L. For inadvertent overdose: start within 1 hour; dose proportional to MTX exposure and renal function.

references.label: FDA label for leucovorin; ASCO and ESMO MTX rescue protocols

poison: High-dose methotrexate with delayed clearance and renal failure
mechanism: Recombinant bacterial enzyme that hydrolyses extracellular methotrexate to inactive metabolites (DAMPA + glutamate), rapidly reducing plasma MTX by >95% within 15 minutes.
dosing: Single IV dose 50 units/kg over 5 minutes. Continue folinic acid (do not give within 2h of glucarpidase). Specialist (oncology / poisons) use only.

references.label: EMA / FDA label for glucarpidase; ASCO HDMTX delayed-clearance guidance

poison: Severe anticholinergic toxicity (Datura, atropine, antihistamine, TCA — restricted, antimuscarinic antiparkinsonian)
mechanism: Tertiary-amine acetylcholinesterase inhibitor that crosses the BBB, restoring central cholinergic transmission and reversing the central anticholinergic syndrome (agitated delirium, hallucinations, hyperthermia).
dosing: Adult: 1–2 mg slow IV over 5 minutes; may repeat every 10–15 min to a total of 4 mg. Cardiac monitoring mandatory; do NOT give in TCA overdose with QRS widening (asystole risk).

references.label: American Academy of Clinical Toxicology / EAPCCT position paper

mechanism: Isoniazid depletes pyridoxal-5-phosphate, halting GABA synthesis and triggering refractory seizures. High-dose pyridoxine restores GABA synthesis and terminates seizures unresponsive to benzodiazepines.
dosing: Adult: pyridoxine 1 g IV per gram of isoniazid ingested (estimate 5 g if unknown amount). Paediatric: 70 mg/kg up to 5 g. Repeat as needed. Give benzodiazepines concurrently.

references.label: Goldfrank's Toxicologic Emergencies; WHO TB chapter

poison: Tricyclic antidepressant overdose with QRS prolongation, hypotension, ventricular arrhythmia
mechanism: Combines sodium loading (which overcomes fast sodium channel blockade) with alkalinisation (which reduces free drug by increasing protein binding and shifts cardiac membrane potential).
dosing: Adult: 1–2 mmol/kg IV bolus of 8.4% sodium bicarbonate when QRS > 100 ms, hypotensive, or in ventricular arrhythmia; repeat boluses until QRS narrows or pH 7.50–7.55; consider infusion.

references.label: American College of Medical Toxicology consensus; UK Toxbase

poison: Amatoxin (Amanita phalloides, A. virosa) mushroom poisoning
antidote: IV silibinin (Legalon SIL) + N-acetylcysteine; supportive penicillin G in some protocols
mechanism: Silibinin competitively inhibits hepatic OATP1B3-mediated amatoxin uptake; NAC supplements glutathione; penicillin G displaces amatoxin from albumin (modest benefit).
dosing: Silibinin 5 mg/kg IV bolus then 20 mg/kg/24h infusion until liver function recovers or transplantation. Start as soon as Amanita exposure is suspected — toxicity peaks 24–48h after ingestion.

references.label: European Association for the Study of the Liver — acute liver failure guidelines

antidote: 100% normobaric oxygen (and hyperbaric oxygen if severe)
mechanism: Increasing alveolar PO2 displaces CO from haemoglobin (reducing half-life of carboxyhaemoglobin from ~5h on room air to ~80 min on 100% O2 and ~20 min in hyperbaric chamber) and prevents delayed neurological sequelae.
dosing: 100% O2 via tight-fitting non-rebreather mask or endotracheal tube for at least 6 hours, or until COHb < 5%. Consider hyperbaric O2 (2.5–3 ATA) for: loss of consciousness, neurological deficit, cardiac ischaemia, pregnancy with COHb > 15%, or COHb > 25%.

references.label: Undersea & Hyperbaric Medical Society CO poisoning guidelines

mechanism: Urinary alkalinisation (urine pH ≥7.5) traps salicylate in ionised form in the renal tubule, dramatically increasing clearance. Haemodialysis is highly effective for severe poisoning.
dosing: Loading: 1–2 mmol/kg sodium bicarbonate IV, then infuse 150 mmol in 1 L 5% dextrose at 1.5–2× maintenance, targeting urine pH 7.5–8.0. Replace potassium aggressively (hypokalaemia prevents alkalinisation). Haemodialysis if level >100 mg/dL (acute), >60 mg/dL with acidosis, AKI, pulmonary oedema, altered mental status, or any level after chronic ingestion with severe features.

references.label: EXTRIP recommendations for salicylate; AACT/EAPCCT urinary alkalinisation

mechanism: Lithium is a small unbound ion freely cleared by dialysis. No chelator exists. Stop lithium, fluid-replete, and dialyse for severe toxicity.
dosing: Haemodialysis indicated if: lithium > 4.0 mmol/L; lithium 2.5–4.0 mmol/L with severe symptoms (seizures, coma, life-threatening arrhythmia, renal failure); chronic toxicity with neurological symptoms. Continue until lithium < 1.0 mmol/L and no rebound after 6h.

references.label: EXTRIP recommendations for lithium poisoning (2015)

mechanism: Reverses vitamin K epoxide reductase inhibition, restoring synthesis of factors II, VII, IX, X.
dosing: Acute bleeding: vitamin K1 10 mg slow IV + 4-factor PCC. Maintenance: oral vitamin K1 50–100 mg/day, titrated to INR; may need weeks to months because of brodifacoum's terminal half-life (~24 days). Monitor INR weekly for 6 months.

references.label: AACT clinical management; UK Toxbase

poison: Life-threatening bleeding on rivaroxaban or apixaban
antidote: Andexanet alfa (preferred where available) or 4-factor prothrombin complex concentrate (PCC, 25–50 IU/kg)
mechanism: Andexanet alfa is a modified recombinant factor Xa decoy that binds and sequesters direct Xa inhibitors. 4-factor PCC bypasses the inhibited factor by raising other vitamin K-dependent factor levels.
dosing: Andexanet alfa: low dose (400 mg bolus then 480 mg infusion over 2h) for low-dose / >8h since last apixaban or rivaroxaban; high dose (800 mg bolus then 960 mg infusion) for high-dose or recent ingestion. 4F-PCC (alternative): 25–50 IU/kg IV.

references.label: ANNEXA-4 trial (andexanet); ACC expert consensus on anticoagulation reversal (2020)

poison: Lead, arsenic, mercury (inorganic and organic) poisoning
antidote: DMSA (succimer) — oral chelator (or BAL / dimercaprol IM for severe/unable-to-take-oral)
mechanism: Water-soluble dithiol chelator that forms a stable, excretable complex with lead, arsenic and mercury, mobilising them from soft tissue and increasing urinary excretion.
dosing: DMSA (succimer) 10 mg/kg PO 8-hourly for 5 days, then 12-hourly for 14 days. For severe poisoning or encephalopathy: dimercaprol (BAL) 3–5 mg/kg IM every 4h + CaNa2EDTA. Lead encephalopathy in children always requires hospital chelation.

references.label: WHO lead poisoning guidance; CDC childhood lead surveillance

poison: Internal contamination with radioactive caesium-137 or thallium
mechanism: Ion-exchange resin that binds caesium and thallium in the gut, interrupting their entero-enteric circulation and accelerating faecal excretion.
dosing: Adults: 3 g PO 3-times daily; children: 1 g 3-times daily. Continue at least 30 days, longer based on whole-body counting / urinary excretion.

references.label: FDA emergency-use guidance; IAEA radiation emergency response

antidote: Bromocriptine + dantrolene (with cessation of offending drug, cooling, supportive care)
mechanism: Bromocriptine is a dopamine agonist that reverses the central dopaminergic blockade of NMS. Dantrolene inhibits sarcoplasmic reticulum calcium release, breaking the muscle rigidity → hyperthermia cycle.
dosing: Bromocriptine 2.5 mg PO/NG 8-hourly, titrated up to 5 mg every 4h. Dantrolene 1–2.5 mg/kg IV initially, repeat to a maximum 10 mg/kg/day. Aggressive cooling, fluids, treat rhabdomyolysis; specialist input.

references.label: Strawn et al. — Neuroleptic Malignant Syndrome (2007); UpToDate (clinical synthesis)

poison: Severe serotonin syndrome (precipitated by SSRI/SNRI + MAOI / linezolid / tramadol / MDMA)
antidote: Cyproheptadine (5-HT2A antagonist) + cessation of serotonergic drugs + supportive cooling and benzodiazepines
mechanism: Cyproheptadine non-specifically blocks central 5-HT2A receptors, reducing the autonomic instability, clonus, hyperthermia and agitation.
dosing: Cyproheptadine 12 mg PO loading dose, then 2 mg every 2h until clinical response; maintenance 8 mg every 6h. Stop offending drug; treat agitation/seizure with benzodiazepines; cool aggressively (target <38.5°C). Intubate and paralyse with non-depolarising relaxant if hyperthermia >41°C.

references.label: Boyer & Shannon — Serotonin Syndrome NEJM (2005); UK Toxbase

poison: Severe inorganic lead poisoning with encephalopathy or very high blood lead
mechanism: CaNa2EDTA chelates extracellular lead, mobilising it for urinary excretion; co-administered BAL prevents redistribution of lead into the CNS during initial chelation.
dosing: Adult/paediatric encephalopathy: BAL IM first, then add CaNa2EDTA by IV infusion per protocol for 5 days; cycle as needed. Specialist (paediatric / toxicology) supervision essential.

references.label: CDC childhood lead exposure case management; Goldfrank's Toxicologic Emergencies

poison: Symptomatic lead poisoning (without encephalopathy) — oral chelation
mechanism: Oral water-soluble dithiol that forms a renally-excreted complex with lead; less risk of redistribution than BAL.
dosing: 10 mg/kg PO every 8h for 5 days, then every 12h for 14 days; repeat course after rebound if levels remain elevated. Confirm lead source eliminated before/during chelation.

references.label: CDC childhood lead surveillance; WHO lead poisoning guidance

poison: Acute or chronic inorganic arsenic poisoning
antidote: DMSA (succimer) — oral; BAL (dimercaprol) IM for severe/unable-to-take-oral
mechanism: Dithiol chelators bind arsenic via sulfhydryl groups, restoring function of enzymes inhibited by arsenic and accelerating urinary excretion.
dosing: DMSA 10 mg/kg PO 8-hourly for 5 days then 12-hourly for 14 days; or BAL 3–5 mg/kg IM every 4h initially for severe poisoning, with transition to DMSA when tolerated.

references.label: Goldfrank's Toxicologic Emergencies; WHO arsenic guidance

antidote: DMSA (succimer) — oral; BAL contraindicated for organic methylmercury
mechanism: DMSA chelates mercury for renal excretion. Note: BAL is contraindicated in organic methylmercury poisoning (redistributes mercury to CNS) — use DMSA only.
dosing: DMSA 10 mg/kg PO 8-hourly for 5 days then 12-hourly for 14 days. For severe inorganic poisoning with renal failure, dialysis with chelator may be needed (specialist input).

references.label: Goldfrank's Toxicologic Emergencies; WHO mercury guidance

mechanism: DMSA chelates organic mercury without the CNS redistribution risk of BAL. Treatment is largely supportive with prolonged elimination of mercury source; recovery from neurological injury is incomplete.
dosing: DMSA per standard schedule; ensure mercury source removed (contaminated fish, occupational). Specialist neurotoxicology input.

references.label: Goldfrank's Toxicologic Emergencies; WHO mercury guidance

mechanism: Penicillamine chelates copper, mobilising hepatic stores for urinary excretion. Trientine is an alternative chelator with a different side-effect profile.
dosing: Penicillamine 250 mg PO 4-times daily titrated to urinary copper response; supplement pyridoxine 25 mg/day. Specialist (hepatology) supervision required.

references.label: EASL Clinical Practice Guidelines on Wilson disease

mechanism: Ion-exchange resin that binds thallium in the gut lumen, disrupting entero-enteric recycling and accelerating faecal elimination.
dosing: Adult: 3 g PO 3-times daily; paediatric: 1 g 3-times daily. Continue until urine thallium is acceptably low. Supportive care for neuropathy and alopecia.

references.label: FDA emergency-use guidance for Prussian blue

poison: Gold salt toxicity (severe mucocutaneous or haematological)
mechanism: Dithiol chelator binds gold, accelerating elimination. Stopping the gold preparation is the primary intervention; chelation reserved for severe toxicity.
dosing: BAL 3 mg/kg IM every 4–6h initially per specialist advice; clinical use is rare now that gold therapy is largely obsolete.

references.label: Goldfrank's Toxicologic Emergencies

antidote: DMSA — discontinuation usually sufficient; chelation for severe disease
mechanism: DMSA chelates bismuth for renal excretion. Bismuth encephalopathy is reversible with cessation in most cases.
dosing: Stop bismuth-containing preparations; DMSA per standard schedule for severe encephalopathy or AKI. Supportive care.

references.label: Goldfrank's Toxicologic Emergencies

antidote: Removal from exposure + supportive care; chelation experimental
mechanism: Manganese deposits in basal ganglia producing a parkinsonian syndrome that responds poorly to chelation; removal from exposure and symptomatic levodopa for parkinsonian features.
dosing: Cessation of exposure; symptomatic management for parkinsonism. CaNa2EDTA has been used experimentally — specialist input.

references.label: Goldfrank's Toxicologic Emergencies

antidote: Supportive care; NAC may reduce oxidative injury
mechanism: Hexavalent chromium is a potent oxidiser causing GI corrosion, AKI, and hepatic injury. No specific chelator; NAC has been used to limit oxidative damage.
dosing: Decontamination; fluid resuscitation; NAC dosing per paracetamol-style protocol has been used (specialist advice). Haemodialysis if AKI.

references.label: Goldfrank's Toxicologic Emergencies

antidote: Supportive care; chelation NOT recommended (worsens renal injury)
mechanism: Cadmium accumulates in renal cortex; chelators (BAL, EDTA) mobilise cadmium to the kidney, worsening nephrotoxicity. Removal from exposure and supportive care only.
dosing: Cessation of exposure; supportive ventilation for acute pneumonitis; renal supportive care. Avoid BAL.

references.label: Goldfrank's Toxicologic Emergencies

antidote: No specific antidote — supportive care, early endoscopy
mechanism: No neutralising agent should be given (heat from neutralisation worsens injury). Do NOT induce vomiting and avoid charcoal. Early endoscopy stratifies injury; proton pump inhibitor and supportive care.
dosing: NPO; analgesia; IV fluids; early upper GI endoscopy within 12–24h; surgical input if perforation. PPI may help.

references.label: ESGE caustic ingestion guidance; UK Toxbase

poison: Button (lithium disc) battery ingestion lodged in oesophagus
mechanism: Lithium disc batteries generate hydroxide at the negative pole, causing rapid oesophageal alkali burn. Honey or sucralfate (children >12 months) may neutralise the local current and slow injury before removal.
dosing: If <12h, age >12 months, asymptomatic, no NPO contraindication: 10 mL honey PO every 10 min up to 6 doses while transferring for endoscopy. Endoscopic removal within 2h ideal.

references.label: National Capital Poison Center / NASPGHAN button battery guideline

antidote: Supportive care — observation; airway protection if depressed conscious level
mechanism: Concentrated surfactants cause CNS depression, vomiting, and respiratory injury from aspiration. No antidote; airway and supportive care.
dosing: Wipe mouth; airway protection; observation for at least 4–6h. Endoscopy if persistent symptoms.

references.label: AAPCC / UK Toxbase paediatric ingestion guidance

poison: Unfractionated heparin over-anticoagulation / cardiac surgery reversal
mechanism: Cationic protamine binds anionic heparin in a 1:1 stoichiometric complex with no anticoagulant activity.
dosing: Approximately 1 mg protamine per 100 units heparin given in the prior 2–3h (reduce if >2h); slow IV to avoid hypotension and anaphylactoid reaction.

references.label: ACC/AHA expert consensus on anticoagulation reversal

mechanism: Protamine neutralises ~60% of LMWH anti-Xa activity (variable by preparation). Half-doses for distant administration; specialist haematology guidance for major bleeding.
dosing: Within 8h: 1 mg protamine per 1 mg enoxaparin (or per 100 anti-Xa units of dalteparin). After 8h: half this dose. Consider 4F-PCC adjunct for major bleeding.

references.label: BSH guidelines on LMWH reversal

antidote: No specific antidote — consider activated PCC (FEIBA) or rFVIIa with haematology input
mechanism: Fondaparinux is a synthetic indirect Xa inhibitor with no specific reverser. Activated PCC (FEIBA) or recombinant factor VIIa can bypass the inhibition; risk of thrombosis must be balanced against bleeding.
dosing: Stop drug; supportive measures, blood products. aPCC (FEIBA) 20 IU/kg or rFVIIa 90 mcg/kg has been used in case series — specialist (haematology) decision.

references.label: ACC expert consensus on anticoagulation reversal (2020)

poison: Major bleeding (especially ICH) on alteplase / tenecteplase thrombolysis
mechanism: Thrombolytics deplete fibrinogen and produce systemic fibrinolysis. Cryoprecipitate replaces fibrinogen (target >150 mg/dL); tranexamic acid blocks ongoing fibrinolysis; platelets if thrombocytopenic.
dosing: Cryoprecipitate 10 units (or 0.15 units/kg) IV; tranexamic acid 10–15 mg/kg IV bolus; platelets if <100 ×10⁹/L. Neurosurgical input for ICH.

references.label: AHA/ASA guidelines for management of symptomatic ICH after thrombolysis (2019)

mechanism: Very large volume of distribution and long half-life (weeks) make removal impossible. Manage bradycardia (atropine, pacing), hypotension (vasopressors), and chronic toxicity (pulmonary, hepatic, thyroid).
dosing: Stop drug; supportive cardiac and respiratory care; thyroid monitoring. Dialysis ineffective.

references.label: UK Toxbase amiodarone monograph

poison: Sotalol-induced torsades de pointes / prolonged QT
antidote: Magnesium sulfate IV (+ overdrive pacing, isoprenaline)
mechanism: Magnesium stabilises cardiac membrane and shortens QT-dependent re-entrant arrhythmia. Overdrive pacing or isoprenaline raises heart rate to shorten QT.
dosing: Magnesium 2 g IV over 10 min, repeat; correct K⁺ to high-normal; overdrive pacing to HR ~ 90; specialist cardiology input.

references.label: AHA/ACLS guidance on torsades; UK Toxbase

poison: Flecainide / Class IC antiarrhythmic toxicity with QRS prolongation
antidote: Sodium bicarbonate (+ lipid emulsion in severe cases)
mechanism: Sodium loading overcomes Na-channel blockade; alkalinisation reduces free drug. IV lipid emulsion sequesters the lipophilic drug for life-threatening collapse.
dosing: 1–2 mmol/kg 8.4% sodium bicarbonate IV bolus for QRS > 100 ms; repeat to QRS narrowing or pH 7.5–7.55. ILE 1.5 mL/kg bolus then infusion for cardiac arrest/refractory collapse.

references.label: UK Toxbase flecainide monograph

antidote: IV dextrose (+ glucagon if no IV access)
mechanism: Replaces glucose; glucagon mobilises hepatic glycogen (ineffective in starvation, liver failure, or alcohol-induced glycogen depletion).
dosing: Adult: 100 mL 20% dextrose IV (or 200 mL 10%); paediatric 2 mL/kg 10% dextrose; follow with infusion. Glucagon 1 mg IM if no IV access. Long insulin overdoses need prolonged infusion and frequent BM checks; admit for observation.

references.label: JBDS-IP / IDF hypoglycaemia guidance

mechanism: Metformin is dialysable; lactate is dialysable. Haemodialysis corrects acidosis and removes drug. Stop metformin; treat shock/sepsis precipitants.
dosing: Haemodialysis if: lactate > 20 mmol/L; pH < 7.0; shock; failure of standard supportive care. Continue until pH > 7.35 and lactate < 3 mmol/L.

references.label: EXTRIP recommendations for metformin poisoning

poison: Bupropion overdose (seizures, QRS widening, QT prolongation)
antidote: Benzodiazepines for seizures; sodium bicarbonate for QRS; supportive
mechanism: Bupropion lowers seizure threshold and blocks cardiac sodium channels (delayed onset of seizures and QRS prolongation up to 24h). No specific antidote; lipid emulsion considered for refractory collapse.
dosing: Benzodiazepine for seizures; 1–2 mmol/kg sodium bicarbonate for QRS > 100 ms; monitor for 24h after sustained-release ingestion.

references.label: UK Toxbase bupropion monograph

poison: Valproate overdose with hyperammonaemia or hepatotoxicity
mechanism: Valproate depletes carnitine, impairing fatty-acid oxidation and inducing hyperammonaemic encephalopathy. L-carnitine restores mitochondrial function and lowers ammonia.
dosing: L-carnitine 100 mg/kg IV bolus then 50 mg/kg every 8h until clinical/biochemical improvement. Haemodialysis for VPA > 850–1000 mg/L, severe encephalopathy, shock, or refractory acidosis.

references.label: EXTRIP recommendations for valproate poisoning

antidote: Multidose activated charcoal + haemodialysis for severe poisoning
mechanism: Theophylline undergoes enterohepatic recirculation; MDAC reduces absorption and reabsorption. Theophylline is highly dialysable; haemodialysis preferred for severe toxicity.
dosing: Activated charcoal 50 g PO every 4h while bowel sounds present. Haemodialysis if level > 100 mg/L (acute), > 60 mg/L (chronic, elderly), seizures, ventricular arrhythmia, or refractory hypotension.

references.label: EXTRIP recommendations for theophylline poisoning

mechanism: Hyaluronidase degrades subcutaneous hyaluronan, dispersing the extravasated vesicant and reducing local tissue concentration. Warm compresses accelerate dispersion.
dosing: Hyaluronidase 150–300 units SC in divided doses around the extravasation site as soon as possible; warm compress 15–20 min, 4×/day for 24–48h. Do NOT cool (worsens vinca injury).

references.label: ESMO–EONS Clinical Practice Guidelines on extravasation

antidote: Dexrazoxane IV (+ cold compress; remove DMSO from older protocols)
mechanism: Dexrazoxane chelates iron and inhibits topoisomerase II-mediated injury at the extravasation site, dramatically reducing tissue necrosis.
dosing: Dexrazoxane 1000 mg/m² IV (max 2000 mg) within 6h of extravasation, then 1000 mg/m² day 2 and 500 mg/m² day 3 — in the contralateral arm. Cold compress between dexrazoxane doses; do NOT apply DMSO concurrently.

references.label: ESMO–EONS Clinical Practice Guidelines on extravasation

antidote: Phentolamine SC (or topical nitroglycerin) infiltrated locally
mechanism: Phentolamine is a competitive alpha-adrenergic antagonist, reversing local vasoconstriction and restoring perfusion to prevent tissue necrosis.
dosing: Phentolamine 5–10 mg in 10–15 mL saline infiltrated subcutaneously around the extravasation site within 12h; alternative: topical 2% nitroglycerin ointment to area.

references.label: ISMP / hospital pharmacy practice guidance on vasopressor extravasation

mechanism: Antibodies neutralise circulating scorpion neurotoxins (sodium channel-active peptides). Improves neuromuscular and autonomic symptoms.
dosing: Per regional protocol and severity grade; have adrenaline ready for hypersensitivity; supportive prazosin / benzodiazepines.

references.label: WHO scorpion sting guidance; regional poison centre protocols

poison: Latrodectus (black widow / button spider) envenomation with severe systemic symptoms
mechanism: Antibodies neutralise alpha-latrotoxin. Most envenomations are managed with supportive care; antivenom reserved for severe pain, autonomic storm, or pregnancy.
dosing: One vial IV per regional protocol; have adrenaline ready. Opioid analgesia, benzodiazepines for muscle spasm.

references.label: AAPCC / regional latrodectus protocols

antidote: Supportive wound care; dapsone debated; antivenom only in some regions
mechanism: Sphingomyelinase D-mediated dermonecrosis; no robust evidence for surgical excision, hyperbaric oxygen or dapsone. Regional antivenoms (South America) may help.
dosing: Local wound care; tetanus prophylaxis; analgesia; monitor for systemic loxoscelism (haemolysis, AKI) — supportive transfusion and renal care.

references.label: AAPCC loxoscelism management; WHO neglected tropical diseases

antidote: CSL box jellyfish antivenom (where available) + vinegar decontamination
mechanism: Antibodies neutralise circulating box jellyfish venom; vinegar inactivates nematocysts on the skin, preventing further envenomation.
dosing: Vinegar (4–6% acetic acid) liberally to all tentacle contact for ≥30 seconds; antivenom IV per local protocol for life-threatening envenomation; analgesia (opioid + Mg for severe pain).

references.label: CSL Behring box jellyfish antivenom labelling; Australian Resuscitation Council guidance

mechanism: Heat (~45°C water immersion 30–90 min) inactivates the heat-labile venom toxin; antivenom for severe systemic envenomation.
dosing: Hot-water immersion 45°C as tolerated; stonefish antivenom IM per vial-count by number of puncture wounds (regional protocol).

references.label: CSL Behring stonefish antivenom; Australian Resuscitation Council

poison: Oleander (Nerium oleander, yellow oleander Cascabela) cardiac glycoside poisoning
antidote: Digoxin-specific Fab fragments (cross-react with plant cardiac glycosides)
mechanism: Plant cardiac glycosides (oleandrin, thevetin) share the steroid-cardenolide moiety recognised by digoxin Fab; Fab binds and neutralises them.
dosing: Empirical 5–10 vials IV for life-threatening arrhythmia or significant hyperkalaemia; serum 'digoxin' level on standard assay cross-reacts and can guide. Higher doses than digoxin overdose often needed.

references.label: WHO yellow oleander poisoning bulletin; UK Toxbase

antidote: No specific antidote — supportive care (sodium bicarbonate, magnesium, lipid emulsion for refractory collapse)
mechanism: Taxine alkaloids block cardiac sodium and calcium channels causing wide-complex bradyarrhythmia and asystole. No antidote; manage as severe sodium-channel blockade with supportive measures.
dosing: Sodium bicarbonate for QRS widening; magnesium; pacing; IV lipid emulsion 1.5 mL/kg bolus then infusion for cardiac arrest. Activated charcoal if recent ingestion.

references.label: UK Toxbase yew monograph; case series

mechanism: Monomethylhydrazine inhibits pyridoxal-5-phosphate-dependent GABA synthesis (same mechanism as isoniazid). High-dose pyridoxine restores GABA and terminates seizures.
dosing: Pyridoxine 70 mg/kg IV (max 5 g) for seizures; repeat as needed. Benzodiazepines concurrently; NAC for hepatic injury per paracetamol-style protocol.

references.label: Goldfrank's Toxicologic Emergencies — mushrooms

antidote: Atropine (small titrated doses to reverse muscarinic excess)
mechanism: Muscarine is a direct muscarinic agonist causing the SLUDGE syndrome (salivation, lacrimation, urination, defecation, GI cramps, emesis). Atropine reverses muscarinic effects.
dosing: Atropine 0.5–1 mg IV titrated to drying of secretions and clear chest; usually small doses sufficient (unlike organophosphate toxicity). Symptoms resolve within hours.

references.label: Goldfrank's Toxicologic Emergencies — mushrooms

antidote: Supportive (reassurance, quiet environment, benzodiazepines for agitation)
mechanism: 5-HT2A agonism. No antidote. Manage anxiety/agitation; observe for hyperthermia.
dosing: Quiet environment; benzodiazepines (e.g. lorazepam 1–2 mg) for severe agitation; observe.

references.label: UK Toxbase psilocybin monograph

poison: Amanita muscaria / pantherina (ibotenic acid / muscimol) poisoning
mechanism: Muscimol is a GABA-A agonist; ibotenic acid is a glutamate analogue. Produces a mixed sedative-delirious picture. Atropine is contraindicated (worsens picture if anticholinergic).
dosing: Benzodiazepines for agitation/seizures; supportive observation. Avoid atropine.

references.label: Goldfrank's Toxicologic Emergencies — mushrooms

antidote: No specific antidote — decontamination + supportive care
mechanism: Ricin is a ribosome-inactivating protein. No effective antidote. Aggressive supportive care for GI necrosis, AKI, hepatic injury; respiratory support for inhalation.
dosing: Decontamination (skin, GI — activated charcoal if recent oral); fluid resuscitation; supportive multi-organ care.

references.label: CDC chemical/biological terrorism — ricin

antidote: Benzodiazepines + non-depolarising paralysis with mechanical ventilation
mechanism: Strychnine antagonises glycine receptors in the spinal cord, producing painful muscle spasms with intact consciousness. Benzodiazepines and (if severe) paralysis with ventilation prevent rhabdomyolysis and asphyxia.
dosing: Quiet, dark environment; benzodiazepines (e.g. diazepam 5–10 mg IV titrated); intubation, neuromuscular blockade and ventilation for severe spasms. Treat rhabdomyolysis aggressively.

references.label: UK Toxbase strychnine monograph

antidote: Supportive — benzodiazepines for seizure, mechanical ventilation for paralysis
mechanism: Coniine is a nicotinic agonist then antagonist producing initial stimulation followed by ascending paralysis (Socrates' death). No antidote; ventilation is life-saving.
dosing: Airway protection and mechanical ventilation as paralysis ascends; supportive care; activated charcoal if recent oral ingestion.

references.label: UK Toxbase hemlock monograph

mechanism: Nitrite induces methaemoglobinaemia, which binds free sulfide. 100% oxygen accelerates dissociation from cytochrome c oxidase. Hydroxocobalamin has been used off-label.
dosing: 100% O2 immediately; sodium nitrite 300 mg IV slow (adult) if severe; hydroxocobalamin 5 g IV considered. Hyperbaric oxygen for severe / persistent neurological injury.

references.label: UK Toxbase H2S monograph; CDC NIOSH

mechanism: Same as organophosphate poisoning but with potent, rapidly-ageing inhibitors. Triple-drug autoinjector kits provide atropine (muscarinic), pralidoxime (oxime — give before ageing), and diazepam (seizure prophylaxis).
dosing: Field: 1–3 ComboPen / DuoDote / Mark I autoinjector kits IM by severity. Hospital: continue atropine (large doses titrated to dry chest), pralidoxime infusion, diazepam 5–10 mg IV for seizures. Decontamination essential.

references.label: WHO chemical incident response; CDC Strategic National Stockpile

antidote: Supportive — bronchodilators, humidified oxygen, NIV / mechanical ventilation
mechanism: Chlorine forms hydrochloric acid in airways causing tracheobronchitis and chemical pneumonitis. No specific antidote; nebulised sodium bicarbonate has been used off-label.
dosing: Remove from exposure; humidified 100% O2; nebulised salbutamol; consider nebulised 4% sodium bicarbonate; observe for 24h (delayed pulmonary oedema).

references.label: UK Toxbase chlorine monograph; CDC NIOSH

antidote: Supportive — prolonged observation for delayed pulmonary oedema
mechanism: Phosgene acylates alveolar proteins producing delayed non-cardiogenic pulmonary oedema (latency 4–48h). No specific antidote. Strict rest reduces oedema progression.
dosing: Remove from exposure; bed rest; humidified O2; observe minimum 24h regardless of symptoms; mechanical ventilation if pulmonary oedema develops.

references.label: UK Toxbase phosgene monograph

antidote: No effective antidote — early activated charcoal / Fuller's earth + avoid supplemental oxygen + early haemoperfusion (variable benefit)
mechanism: Paraquat produces redox-cycling oxidative lung injury with progressive pulmonary fibrosis. Supplemental oxygen exacerbates injury — avoid unless SpO2 < 88%. Charcoal / Fuller's earth limits absorption. Haemoperfusion offers limited benefit.
dosing: Avoid supplemental oxygen if not hypoxaemic. Activated charcoal 1 g/kg or Fuller's earth 15% suspension; early haemoperfusion within 2–4h has been used. Glucocorticoids and cyclophosphamide use is debated. Prognosis poor for significant ingestions.

references.label: WHO paraquat poisoning guidance; UK Toxbase

antidote: Atropine only — pralidoxime NOT routinely indicated
mechanism: Carbamates reversibly inhibit acetylcholinesterase (spontaneous reactivation within hours — no ageing). Atropine reverses muscarinic effects; pralidoxime is generally not needed and may worsen toxicity in pure carbamate poisoning.
dosing: Atropine titrated to dry secretions and clear chest, smaller total doses than organophosphate; supportive care. Pralidoxime only if mixed carbamate-organophosphate ingestion.

references.label: WHO carbamate guidance; UK Toxbase

antidote: Supportive — topical vitamin E for paraesthesia; benzodiazepines for seizures
mechanism: Pyrethroids prolong sodium channel opening. Most exposures cause only paraesthesia (topical) or nausea (oral); seizures rare. No specific antidote.
dosing: Wash skin; topical vitamin E oil for facial paraesthesia; benzodiazepines for seizures; supportive observation.

references.label: UK Toxbase pyrethroid monograph

mechanism: Selective agonist at insect nicotinic acetylcholine receptors. Human toxicity usually mild (GI, drowsiness); severe ingestion may produce hypotension, seizures, respiratory failure.
dosing: Supportive; benzodiazepines for seizures; fluid and pressor support for hypotension. Activated charcoal if recent ingestion.

references.label: UK Toxbase neonicotinoid monograph; WHO IPCS

antidote: Supportive — airway, thiamine before glucose, dextrose for hypoglycaemia
mechanism: No reversal agent. Manage airway, prevent aspiration, treat hypoglycaemia, give thiamine before glucose to prevent Wernicke's encephalopathy in chronic users.
dosing: Airway management; thiamine 100–250 mg IV/IM before glucose; dextrose if BM low; observe until clinically sober. Haemodialysis only for extreme ingestion / coma not improving.

references.label: UK Toxbase ethanol monograph

antidote: Folinic acid (or folate) to accelerate formate metabolism + fomepizole + dialysis
mechanism: Folinic acid (or folate) is a cofactor for tetrahydrofolate-dependent oxidation of formate to CO2, accelerating clearance of the toxic metabolite. Always combined with fomepizole / ethanol blockade and haemodialysis for significant exposure.
dosing: Folinic acid 1 mg/kg IV (max 50 mg) every 4–6h until methanol and formate cleared. Co-administer fomepizole; arrange haemodialysis for level > 50 mg/dL, acidosis, visual symptoms, or AKI.

references.label: EXTRIP recommendations for methanol; AACT/EAPCCT methanol position paper

antidote: Thiamine + pyridoxine to redirect metabolism + fomepizole + dialysis
mechanism: Thiamine and pyridoxine are cofactors that redirect glyoxylate to non-toxic metabolites (alpha-hydroxy-beta-ketoadipate and glycine) rather than oxalate. Combine with fomepizole / ethanol blockade and haemodialysis.
dosing: Thiamine 100 mg IV every 6h; pyridoxine 50 mg IV every 6h. Fomepizole as per protocol. Dialysis for severe acidosis, AKI, or significant exposure.

references.label: EXTRIP recommendations for ethylene glycol; AACT/EAPCCT position paper

antidote: Supportive — no fomepizole indicated (no toxic metabolite); dialysis for severe coma / hypotension
mechanism: Metabolised to acetone (CNS depressant; no acidosis). Distinguishes from methanol/EG by ketosis without acidosis. No need for ADH blockade.
dosing: Airway protection; IV fluids; haemodialysis only for refractory hypotension, coma, or very high levels.

references.label: UK Toxbase isopropyl monograph

poison: Propylene glycol toxicity (high-dose IV diluent — lorazepam, phenobarbital infusions)
antidote: Stop infusion; supportive — dialysis for severe lactic acidosis / AKI
mechanism: Propylene glycol is metabolised to lactate; large IV doses (from solvent in lorazepam, phenobarbital, diazepam infusions) cause anion-gap acidosis. Stop infusion; dialysis if severe.
dosing: Stop the carrier infusion; switch to alternative formulation; supportive; haemodialysis for severe acidosis or AKI.

references.label: ISMP / hospital pharmacy practice guidance

poison: Chronic iron overload (transfusion-dependent thalassaemia, sickle cell)
mechanism: Oral tridentate chelator forms a stable complex with ferric iron for biliary excretion. Used for chronic iron overload — not for acute iron poisoning.
dosing: Deferasirox 14–28 mg/kg/day (film-coated tablet) titrated to ferritin. Monitor renal function, LFTs, hearing, vision. Specialist (haematology) supervision.

references.label: Thalassaemia International Federation guidelines; UK BSH iron-overload guidance

poison: Chronic iron overload — alternative oral chelator
mechanism: Bidentate oral chelator with good penetration into cardiac myocytes; particularly used where cardiac iron overload predominates. Risk of agranulocytosis.
dosing: Deferiprone 75–100 mg/kg/day divided 3-times daily. Weekly FBC mandatory (agranulocytosis risk). Specialist supervision.

references.label: Thalassaemia International Federation guidelines

mechanism: Dapsone (and its hydroxylamine metabolite) produces sustained methaemoglobinaemia; methylene blue reduces metHb but may also cause haemolysis in G6PD deficiency. Cimetidine reduces ongoing metHb formation; ascorbic acid for milder cases.
dosing: Methylene blue 1–2 mg/kg IV over 5 min; repeat if needed. Consider cimetidine and ascorbic acid. Stop dapsone; exchange transfusion if severe and G6PD-deficient.

references.label: UK Toxbase dapsone monograph

antidote: No specific antidote — supportive (Fab fragments investigational and not generally available)
mechanism: Colchicine binds tubulin disrupting mitosis with multi-organ failure (GI, marrow, cardiovascular collapse). Triphasic course; specific Fab fragments have been used in limited cases.
dosing: Aggressive supportive care: fluids, vasopressors, G-CSF for marrow suppression. Activated charcoal if early. Specialist (poisons centre) input; very high mortality once cardiovascular phase begins.

references.label: UK Toxbase colchicine monograph

poison: Beta-2-agonist toxicity (high-dose salbutamol — tachycardia, hypokalaemia, lactic acidosis)
antidote: Cautious beta-blocker (selective) + potassium repletion — only for severe symptoms
mechanism: Selective beta-1 blockade reverses tachycardia and beta-2 effects. Use cautiously in asthmatics. Most cases respond to drug cessation and supportive care.
dosing: Stop beta-agonist; replace potassium aggressively (often large doses); cardioselective beta-blocker (e.g. metoprolol 2.5–5 mg IV) only if severe tachyarrhythmia and not in active asthma.

references.label: UK Toxbase salbutamol monograph

antidote: Dantrolene + immediate cessation of trigger + active cooling + supportive
mechanism: Dantrolene inhibits sarcoplasmic reticulum ryanodine receptor calcium release, breaking the muscle contraction → heat → rhabdomyolysis cycle.
dosing: Dantrolene 2.5 mg/kg IV bolus, repeat every 5–10 min to 10 mg/kg (or more if needed). Stop all volatile agents and succinylcholine; switch to TIVA / non-triggering; hyperventilate with 100% O2; active cooling; treat hyperkalaemia, acidosis, rhabdomyolysis.

references.label: MHAUS / EMHG malignant hyperthermia guidance

antidote: Thiamine BEFORE glucose + IV dextrose + fluid resuscitation
mechanism: Thiamine deficiency in chronic alcohol use predisposes to Wernicke's encephalopathy; giving glucose before thiamine can precipitate it. Dextrose and fluid resuscitation reverse the ketoacidosis driven by starvation/dehydration.
dosing: Thiamine 250–500 mg IV (Pabrinex 2 pairs three times daily for 2–3 days) before any glucose. Then 5% dextrose in saline; IV fluid resuscitation; replace K⁺, Mg²⁺, PO4³⁻.

references.label: RCPath / NICE alcohol-related guidance; UK Toxbase

mechanism: Benzodiazepines reduce central sympathetic drive, agitation, hypertension, tachycardia and seizure risk. Pure beta-blockade is avoided (unopposed alpha-stimulation worsens hypertension); mixed alpha-beta blockade (labetalol) or vasodilators preferred for refractory hypertension.
dosing: Diazepam 5–10 mg IV every 5–10 min titrated to sedation. Active cooling for hyperthermia. GTN / phentolamine for refractory hypertension. Lipid emulsion for collapse with cardiac arrest. Avoid pure beta-blockers.

references.label: UK Toxbase cocaine/amphetamine monographs

antidote: Supportive — observe for QT prolongation (citalopram), seizures
mechanism: Most SSRIs in monoingestion are well-tolerated. Citalopram and escitalopram prolong QT (dose-dependent); seizures occur at high doses. Watch for serotonin syndrome with co-ingestants.
dosing: Activated charcoal if early; ECG monitoring for citalopram > 600 mg or escitalopram > 300 mg ingestion (12–24h); benzodiazepines for seizure; treat torsades with magnesium.

references.label: UK Toxbase SSRI monographs

antidote: Supportive — benzodiazepines, fluids; avoid Class IA/III antiarrhythmics
mechanism: Sedation, hypotension, QT prolongation, anticholinergic effects, occasional seizures. Mainly supportive. Watch for NMS with chronic / titrated dosing.
dosing: Airway support; fluids and noradrenaline (avoid pure alpha-agonists in alpha-blocked patient); benzodiazepines for seizures; magnesium for torsades. Lipid emulsion considered for refractory collapse on lipophilic agents.

references.label: UK Toxbase antipsychotic monographs

antidote: Supportive airway management (no specific antidote; flumazenil and naloxone ineffective)
mechanism: GABA-B and GHB receptor agonism produces profound but typically short-lasting (2–4h) CNS depression. Airway protection until self-clears; specific antagonists not clinically available.
dosing: Airway protection and recovery position; intubation if GCS < 8 and not improving; observe until clinically clear. Beware co-ingestion (alcohol, benzodiazepines).

references.label: UK Toxbase GHB monograph

antidote: Supportive — benzodiazepines for agitation; no reversal agent
mechanism: NMDA antagonism. Most ingestions self-resolve; manage agitation and airway. Chronic high-dose use causes ulcerative cystitis.
dosing: Quiet environment; benzodiazepines for agitation; airway protection if depressed; observe.

references.label: UK Toxbase ketamine monograph

antidote: Multi-dose activated charcoal + supportive; haemodialysis for severe
mechanism: Carbamazepine undergoes enterohepatic recirculation; MDAC interrupts this and accelerates clearance. Severe toxicity (seizures, coma, cardiotoxicity) may need extracorporeal removal.
dosing: MDAC 50 g every 4h if bowel sounds present. Haemodialysis (high-flux/high-efficiency) for refractory seizures, persistent coma, cardiotoxicity, or level > 40 mg/L.

references.label: EXTRIP recommendations for carbamazepine

antidote: Multi-dose activated charcoal + urinary alkalinisation; haemodialysis for severe
mechanism: Alkaline urine ion-traps phenobarbital, enhancing renal clearance. MDAC reduces ongoing absorption. Severe cases benefit from haemodialysis.
dosing: MDAC every 4h; sodium bicarbonate to urine pH ≥ 7.5; replace K⁺. Haemodialysis for prolonged coma, hypotension, or very high levels.

references.label: EXTRIP recommendations for barbiturates

antidote: Supportive (overdose); IV/intrathecal reintroduction (acute withdrawal); dialysis for severe overdose
mechanism: GABA-B agonist. Overdose causes profound coma and respiratory depression; abrupt withdrawal of intrathecal baclofen causes life-threatening dysautonomia. Acute overdose responds to airway support; haemodialysis effective in renal failure.
dosing: Airway support; mechanical ventilation as needed; haemodialysis for severe coma especially with AKI. For withdrawal (intrathecal pump failure): emergency restart, benzodiazepines, cyproheptadine for refractory dysautonomia.

references.label: UK Toxbase baclofen monograph

antidote: Supportive — naloxone has been tried (variable response); atropine for bradycardia
mechanism: Alpha-2 central agonism causes hypotension, bradycardia, miosis, sedation (opioid-like). Naloxone trials show variable benefit. Mainly supportive.
dosing: Atropine for symptomatic bradycardia; fluids and vasopressors for hypotension; naloxone 2 mg IV trial (response variable). Observe ≥ 24h for sustained-release.

references.label: UK Toxbase clonidine monograph

antidote: Supportive — manage seizures, serotonin syndrome, cardiotoxicity
mechanism: SNRI overdose can cause seizures, QRS widening (sodium-channel effect at high dose), and serotonin syndrome with co-ingestants. Manage as per individual features.
dosing: Benzodiazepines for seizures; sodium bicarbonate for QRS prolongation; cyproheptadine for severe serotonin syndrome; supportive.

references.label: UK Toxbase venlafaxine monograph

mechanism: Anticholinergic agents reverse the dopamine-blockade-mediated extrapyramidal reaction.
dosing: Adult: procyclidine 5–10 mg IV/IM; alternative benzatropine 1–2 mg IV/IM. Stop offending drug; observe.

references.label: UK Toxbase / BNF on extrapyramidal reactions

mechanism: Absorption of hypotonic glycine irrigation produces dilutional hyponatraemia, hyperammonaemia, visual disturbance. Stop irrigation; correct Na⁺ cautiously; supportive.
dosing: Stop irrigation immediately; 3% hypertonic saline for severe symptomatic hyponatraemia per standard correction limits; supportive for visual / neurological symptoms.

references.label: Hospital pharmacy practice; BAUS guidance on TUR syndrome

mechanism: Free fluoride ion chelates calcium and magnesium, causing local tissue necrosis, hypocalcaemia, hypomagnesaemia, hyperkalaemia and cardiac arrhythmias. Calcium binds and neutralises fluoride.
dosing: Topical 2.5% calcium gluconate gel to skin burns; subcutaneous infiltration of 5% calcium gluconate for digital burns; intra-arterial calcium gluconate for refractory pain; IV calcium for systemic toxicity. Aggressive Mg, K, ECG monitoring.

references.label: UK Toxbase HF burns guidance

antidote: Oral magnesium / sodium sulphate (precipitates insoluble barium sulphate) + K⁺ repletion
mechanism: Sulphate precipitates barium to insoluble (and non-absorbable) barium sulphate. Profound hypokalaemia (intracellular shift) needs aggressive K⁺ replacement. Cardiac monitoring essential.
dosing: Magnesium sulphate or sodium sulphate 30 g PO in adults (1 g/kg paediatric) to bind unabsorbed barium; potassium replacement IV titrated to ECG; supportive haemodialysis if severe.

references.label: UK Toxbase barium monograph

poison: Nitrite / nitrate-induced methaemoglobinaemia (in infants — 'blue baby syndrome')
mechanism: Nitrates converted to nitrites oxidise haemoglobin (Fe2+ to Fe3+). Methylene blue accelerates reduction via NADPH-methaemoglobin reductase.
dosing: Methylene blue 1–2 mg/kg IV over 5 min for symptomatic methHb (typically > 20–30%); careful G6PD assessment.

references.label: UK Toxbase nitrate/nitrite monographs

antidote: Stop drug + vasodilator (nitroprusside / nitroglycerin) for severe ischaemia
mechanism: Ergot alkaloids are potent vasoconstrictors causing peripheral ischaemia and gangrene. No specific antidote; vasodilators reverse vasospasm; anticoagulation may help prevent thrombosis.
dosing: Stop ergot; IV nitroprusside or nitroglycerin titrated to limb perfusion; consider heparin; vascular surgery input for established gangrene.

references.label: UK Toxbase ergotamine monograph

poison: Ethylene-glycol-containing antifreeze (paediatric / veterinary scenario in households)
antidote: Fomepizole or ethanol + thiamine + pyridoxine + dialysis
mechanism: As ethylene-glycol entry above. Paediatric exposures are common from accessible household antifreeze; rapid recognition critical (any unexplained anion-gap acidosis, oxalate crystalluria).
dosing: Fomepizole loading 15 mg/kg IV then per protocol; thiamine + pyridoxine; haemodialysis for significant exposure. Empirical fomepizole if methanol/EG suspected and confirmation will be delayed.

references.label: EXTRIP recommendations for ethylene glycol

poison: Severe cytokine release syndrome (CAR-T, bispecific therapy, severe infection)
mechanism: IL-6 is the central cytokine in CRS; tocilizumab blocks the receptor, rapidly improving fever, hypotension and hypoxia. Corticosteroids added for severe / neurotoxic features (ICANS).
dosing: Tocilizumab 8 mg/kg IV (max 800 mg) for grade ≥ 2 CRS; may repeat once. Add dexamethasone 10 mg IV every 6h for grade ≥ 3 or ICANS.

references.label: ASTCT consensus CRS grading / management

antidote: Stop drug + supportive — manage raised intracranial pressure / hepatotoxicity
mechanism: Acute or chronic excess produces pseudotumor cerebri, hepatotoxicity, mucocutaneous changes. No antidote; cessation and supportive care.
dosing: Stop the supplement / retinoid; manage raised ICP (acetazolamide, lumbar puncture if needed); ophthalmology / neurology input.

references.label: UK Toxbase vitamin A monograph

antidote: Fluids + loop diuretic + corticosteroid + bisphosphonate / calcitonin for severe
mechanism: Excess vitamin D raises intestinal calcium absorption causing hypercalcaemia. Treatment is hypercalcaemia management; corticosteroids reduce 1,25-vitamin D production.
dosing: Saline rehydration; furosemide once euvolaemic; prednisolone 20–40 mg/day; calcitonin 4 IU/kg q12h; zoledronate 4 mg IV for severe / refractory.

references.label: Endocrine Society hypercalcaemia guidance; UK Toxbase

poison: Warfarin / VKA major bleeding (intracranial, GI, retroperitoneal)
antidote: 4-factor prothrombin complex concentrate + IV vitamin K
mechanism: 4F-PCC immediately replaces factors II, VII, IX, X. IV vitamin K (5–10 mg) sustains correction by restoring hepatic synthesis (effect within 6–12h).
dosing: 4F-PCC 25–50 IU/kg by INR / weight; IV vitamin K 5–10 mg slow. Recheck INR at 30 min. FFP only if PCC unavailable.

references.label: BSH guidance on emergency warfarin reversal; ACC consensus 2020

poison: Warfarin / VKA with elevated INR but minor / no bleeding
mechanism: Low-dose oral vitamin K corrects INR within 24h without complete VKA reversal (preserves ability to restart). PCC reserved for major bleeding.
dosing: INR 4.5–10 with no bleeding: withhold warfarin, consider oral vitamin K 1–2.5 mg. INR > 10 no bleeding: withhold + oral vitamin K 2.5–5 mg. INR therapeutic + minor bleeding: hold, vitamin K only if needed.

references.label: BSH and ACCP warfarin management guidance

antidote: Stop infusion, aspirate, mark area, elevate; cold for most (warm for vinca alkaloids)
mechanism: Cooling reduces local diffusion of vesicant (anthracyclines, alkylators) into surrounding tissue. WARM for vinca alkaloids (promotes dispersal). Specific antidotes per agent (dexrazoxane, hyaluronidase, DMSO).
dosing: Stop infusion, aspirate via cannula before removal; mark / photograph; elevate limb. Cold compress 15–20 min, 4×/day for 24–48h (most agents). Specific antidote per drug.

references.label: ESMO–EONS Clinical Practice Guidelines on extravasation

mechanism: Quinolones impair tenocyte collagen synthesis (especially Achilles), with risk amplified by age > 60, corticosteroid co-use, transplant recipients. No antidote.
dosing: Stop quinolone immediately at first sign of tendinopathy; rest, immobilise the affected tendon; orthopaedic referral if rupture suspected. Avoid future fluoroquinolone use.

references.label: FDA / EMA fluoroquinolone safety review; BNF cautions

mechanism: Highly water-soluble irritant gas producing immediate upper-airway and ocular injury. No antidote; airway protection and supportive care.
dosing: Remove from exposure; copious eye and skin irrigation; humidified O2; nebulised salbutamol; intubation if airway oedema developing.

references.label: UK Toxbase ammonia monograph

poison: Smoke inhalation (combined CO + cyanide + irritant gases)
antidote: 100% O2 + empirical hydroxocobalamin for cyanide if shock/acidosis + airway management
mechanism: Combustion of synthetic polymers generates cyanide and CO simultaneously; shocked / acidotic smoke-inhalation victims may have toxic cyanide levels. Hydroxocobalamin can be given empirically (does not interfere with CO management).
dosing: 100% O2 immediately; intubate for stridor, soot in oropharynx, severe inhalation; hydroxocobalamin 5 g IV (paeds 70 mg/kg) for hypotension / lactate > 10 / loss of consciousness; consider hyperbaric O2 for severe COHb.

references.label: European Resuscitation Council; UK Toxbase

poison: Tetrodotoxin (puffer fish, blue-ringed octopus, some newts)
antidote: Supportive — mechanical ventilation until toxin clears
mechanism: Sodium-channel blocker producing ascending paralysis with intact consciousness. No antivenom; ventilatory support is life-saving until toxin clears (24–72h).
dosing: Airway protection, intubation and ventilation as paralysis ascends; supportive care; activated charcoal if recent ingestion.

references.label: WHO marine biotoxins; UK Toxbase

antidote: Supportive (mannitol benefit uncertain; gabapentin / amitriptyline for neuropathy)
mechanism: Ciguatoxin activates voltage-gated sodium channels causing GI symptoms then characteristic cold allodynia and neuropathic pain. No proven antidote; IV mannitol used historically but evidence weak.
dosing: Supportive rehydration; gabapentin or amitriptyline for prolonged neuropathic symptoms; avoid alcohol, fish, nuts for months (recurrence trigger).

references.label: WHO marine biotoxins; CDC ciguatera guidance

mechanism: Bacterial decarboxylation of histidine in spoilt fish produces histamine — mimics anaphylaxis but no IgE involvement. H1 + H2 blockade resolves symptoms rapidly.
dosing: Chlorphenamine 10 mg IV/IM + ranitidine 50 mg IV (or oral cetirizine 10 mg + famotidine 20 mg); usually resolves within hours.

references.label: WHO marine biotoxins; UK Toxbase

antidote: Monovalent coral snake antivenom + ventilation support
mechanism: Coral snake venom is primarily neurotoxic causing delayed descending paralysis. Antivenom prevents progression; once paralysis established, mechanical ventilation until recovery (may be days).
dosing: Antivenom early per regional protocol; intubation and ventilation for established neuromuscular weakness. Have adrenaline ready for antivenom reactions.

references.label: WHO snake antivenom guidance; regional poison centres

antidote: Regional polyvalent / monovalent elapid antivenom + supportive ventilation
mechanism: Elapid venoms produce neurotoxicity (post-synaptic neuromuscular blockade) with risk of respiratory paralysis. Antivenom neutralises circulating toxin; intubation may still be needed.
dosing: Antivenom IV per regional protocol; ventilation for respiratory paralysis until toxin clears or antivenom takes effect. Have adrenaline ready.

references.label: WHO snake antivenom guidance; regional protocols

poison: Viperid (Russell's viper, saw-scaled viper, rattlesnake) envenomation with coagulopathy
antidote: Regional polyvalent viperid antivenom + blood product support
mechanism: Viperid venoms produce venom-induced consumption coagulopathy, AKI, capillary leak. Antivenom neutralises circulating toxins; blood products replace fibrinogen, platelets if bleeding.
dosing: Antivenom IV per regional protocol; 20-minute whole-blood clotting test to track response and re-dose; supportive blood products only if active bleeding (factor replacement otherwise consumed by ongoing venom activity).

references.label: WHO snake antivenom guidance; SE Asia/Africa regional protocols

antidote: Hot-water immersion + analgesia + tetanus + wound exploration
mechanism: Heat (~45°C 30–90 min) inactivates the heat-labile venom protein. Wound exploration / X-ray to find retained barb; tetanus, antibiotics for marine wound pathogens.
dosing: Hot-water immersion 45°C as tolerated; analgesia; explore for retained spine; tetanus update; consider doxycycline + ciprofloxacin cover for Vibrio if seawater exposure.

references.label: Australian Resuscitation Council marine envenomation; CDC marine wounds

poison: Aconite (Aconitum napellus, monkshood — traditional medicine) toxicity
antidote: Supportive — antiarrhythmics (amiodarone), sodium bicarbonate, lipid emulsion for refractory arrest
mechanism: Aconitine activates voltage-gated sodium channels producing refractory ventricular tachyarrhythmia and bradyarrhythmia. No specific antidote; manage as severe sodium-channel poisoning.
dosing: Amiodarone or magnesium for arrhythmia; sodium bicarbonate; lipid emulsion 1.5 mL/kg bolus + infusion for cardiac arrest; cardiopulmonary support (ECMO has been used).

references.label: UK Toxbase aconite monograph; HK regional case series

antidote: Immobilisation + pressure-immobilisation bandage (selected elapids) + rapid transport — antivenom in hospital
mechanism: Pre-hospital care minimises venom spread (elapid neurotoxins) and tissue injury (viperid cytotoxins). Avoid tourniquets, incision, suction. Pressure-immobilisation bandage useful for neurotoxic elapids in Australia / SE Asia but NOT for cytotoxic viperids.
dosing: Remove from danger; immobilise the limb at heart level; pressure-immobilisation bandage for neurotoxic elapid bites (Australian guidance); rapid transport to facility with antivenom. Do NOT incise, suction, apply tourniquet, or attempt to capture snake.

references.label: WHO snake antivenom guidance; Australian Resuscitation Council

antidote: Andexanet alfa (off-label for edoxaban) or 4-factor PCC
mechanism: Edoxaban is a direct factor Xa inhibitor. Andexanet alfa is licensed for apixaban/rivaroxaban but evidence supports use for edoxaban. 4F-PCC is the widely-available alternative.
dosing: Andexanet alfa off-label dosing per recent ingestion (similar to rivaroxaban scheme) or 4F-PCC 25–50 IU/kg. Specialist (haematology) decision.

references.label: ACC expert consensus on anticoagulation reversal (2020)

mechanism: Acts as a sulfur donor for the endogenous enzyme rhodanese (thiosulfate sulfurtransferase), which transfers sulfur to cyanide to form the relatively non-toxic, renally-excreted thiocyanate. Onset is slow, so it is usually combined with a faster-acting antidote (sodium nitrite or hydroxocobalamin).
dosing: Conventionally part of the cyanide antidote kit, given IV after/with sodium nitrite; doses transcribed from local protocol/label (e.g. 12.5 g IV in adults). Repeat at half dose if poisoning recurs.

references.label: Sodium thiosulfate (antidote) monograph; CHEMM/HHS countermeasure database; WHO antidote guidance

mechanism: Oxidises haemoglobin to methaemoglobin, whose ferric iron preferentially binds cyanide as cyanomethaemoglobin, drawing cyanide off cytochrome oxidase; also generates nitric oxide. Given before sodium thiosulfate in the classic cyanide antidote kit.
dosing: Adult 300 mg IV (10 mL of 3% solution); reduce dose with anaemia and use caution in young infants (fetal haemoglobin) and smoke-inhalation victims (avoid excessive methaemoglobin). Doses per label/local protocol.

references.label: Sodium nitrite injection FDA label; CHEMM/HHS countermeasure database; WHO antidote guidance

poison: Cyanide poisoning (first aid, when IV access unavailable)
mechanism: Inhaled nitrite induces some methaemoglobin (which binds cyanide) and causes vasodilation; produces only ~5% methaemoglobin so is a temporising first-aid measure superseded by IV sodium nitrite or hydroxocobalamin.
dosing: Crush 1 ampoule into gauze and have the patient inhale ~30 seconds per minute as a stopgap until definitive IV antidote; largely historical where hydroxocobalamin is available. Per local protocol.

references.label: CHEMM/HHS amyl nitrite countermeasure; Goldfrank's Toxicologic Emergencies

mechanism: Cobalt forms stable, relatively non-toxic complexes directly with cyanide, removing it from cytochrome oxidase faster than methaemoglobin-forming antidotes. Itself toxic (seizures, hypotension, airway oedema) if given without significant cyanide present.
dosing: Reserved for confirmed serious cyanide poisoning; given IV per label/local protocol followed by glucose. Avoid empirically without confirmed exposure due to cobalt toxicity.

references.label: Hall AH et al. Cyanide antidotes in clinical use: dicobalt EDTA (Kelocyanor); UK Toxbase

mechanism: Insulin improves myocardial contractility via PI3K signalling and corrects the impaired myocardial glucose uptake/utilisation caused by CCB/BB toxicity; positive inotropy without raising systemic vascular resistance. Onset of inotropic effect takes 20-30 minutes.
dosing: Regular insulin bolus 1 unit/kg with dextrose 0.5 g/kg, then infusion 1 unit/kg/hour titrated upward; co-administer dextrose and monitor for hypoglycaemia and hypokalaemia. Doses per toxicology protocol.

references.label: Engebretsen KM et al. High-dose insulin therapy in beta-blocker and CCB poisoning. Clin Toxicol; LITFL CCC toxicology

antidote: IV calcium (calcium chloride vs calcium gluconate)
mechanism: Increasing extracellular calcium partially overcomes CCB blockade of L-type calcium channels. Calcium chloride 10% delivers ~3x the elemental calcium of calcium gluconate 10% per gram but is a vesicant requiring central access; gluconate is safer peripherally.
dosing: Calcium chloride 10% (preferably central line) or calcium gluconate 10% (peripheral) repeated/infused with ionised-calcium monitoring; a temporising measure pending inotropes/HIET. Doses per protocol.

references.label: St-Onge M et al. Calcium-channel blocker toxicity management; Goldfrank's Toxicologic Emergencies

poison: Severe hyperkalaemia with ECG changes (incl. drug-induced)
mechanism: Calcium raises the cardiac myocyte action-potential threshold and restores conduction velocity in hyperkalaemia ('membrane stabilisation'), protecting against malignant arrhythmia. It does NOT lower serum potassium, so shift/removal therapies are needed alongside.
dosing: Calcium gluconate 10% 10-30 mL IV over 2-5 min (or calcium chloride 10% via central access), repeat in 5-10 min if ECG changes persist; onset ~3 min, duration 30-60 min. Doses per protocol.

references.label: Calcium gluconate StatPearls; ACEP hyperkalaemia pharmacology resource

poison: Arsenic, mercury and other heavy-metal poisoning
mechanism: Water-soluble dithiol derivative of dimercaprol; its two thiol groups chelate arsenic, mercury, bismuth and other heavy metals into water-soluble complexes excreted in urine. Can be given orally or IV (unlike intramuscular-only BAL).
dosing: Oral or IV per protocol for arsenic and mercury poisoning; specialist/poison-centre guided. Transcribe doses from local antidote guidance.

references.label: Kosnett MJ. The role of chelation in arsenic and mercury poisoning; unithiol (DMPS) literature

poison: Arsenic, inorganic mercury, gold and acute lead encephalopathy
mechanism: Dithiol chelator whose two sulfhydryl groups bind heavy metals (arsenic, mercury, gold, lead), forming complexes excreted renally; lipophilic so penetrates the CNS, used with EDTA in acute lead encephalopathy. Given by painful IM injection.
dosing: Deep IM injection per protocol (e.g. with calcium disodium EDTA in lead encephalopathy); monitor renal function and blood pressure. Transcribe doses from local guidance.

references.label: Dimercaprol StatPearls; Goldfrank's Toxicologic Emergencies

mechanism: Oral chelator that binds copper, lead and mercury, increasing their urinary excretion; in Wilson disease it also induces hepatic metallothionein. Co-administer pyridoxine (vitamin B6) because penicillamine antagonises it.
dosing: Oral, titrated upward per protocol (with pyridoxine supplementation); largely superseded by DMSA for paediatric lead poisoning. Transcribe doses from local guidance.

references.label: Penicillamine StatPearls; AASLD Wilson disease guidance

poison: Internal contamination with plutonium, americium or curium
mechanism: DTPA chelates transuranic elements by ion exchange (its calcium or zinc is replaced by plutonium/americium/curium), forming stable complexes rapidly excreted in urine. Ca-DTPA is ~10x more effective in the first 24 hours; efficacy falls as metal deposits in bone/liver.
dosing: IV (or nebulised for inhalation contamination) as early as possible after exposure, per radiation-emergency protocol; Ca-DTPA first then Zn-DTPA for prolonged courses. Doses per label/REMM guidance.

references.label: CDC/REMM DTPA radiation countermeasure guidance; FDA pentetate calcium/zinc trisodium label

poison: Methanol or ethylene glycol poisoning (when fomepizole unavailable)
mechanism: Competitively inhibits alcohol dehydrogenase, for which it has far higher affinity than methanol/ethylene glycol, preventing formation of toxic metabolites (formate; glycolate/oxalate). Less convenient than fomepizole (requires level monitoring, causes intoxication).
dosing: Loading then maintenance infusion titrated to a target blood ethanol concentration that saturates alcohol dehydrogenase; co-treat with cofactors and dialysis. Doses per toxicology protocol.

references.label: McMartin K et al. Antidotes for poisoning by alcohols that form toxic metabolites. Br J Clin Pharmacol 2016

mechanism: Competitively inhibits hepatocyte uptake of amatoxin via the OATP1B3 (and NTCP) transporters, interrupting enterohepatic recirculation and reducing hepatocyte exposure; high-dose penicillin G works by the same transporter mechanism but is weaker.
dosing: IV silibinin per protocol alongside N-acetylcysteine and aggressive supportive care; transcribe doses from local antidote guidance.

references.label: Letschert K et al. Inhibition of amanitin uptake into human hepatocytes. Toxicol Sci 2006; Legalon SIL data

poison: Botulism (foodborne, wound, adult intestinal — toxin types A-G)
mechanism: Equine-derived antibody fragments bind and clear circulating botulinum neurotoxin (all seven serotypes A-G) before it binds nerve terminals; neutralises only free toxin, so it limits progression but does not reverse established paralysis — give as early as possible.
dosing: Single IV infusion per label/public-health protocol; give early on clinical suspicion without waiting for confirmation. Anaphylaxis precautions (equine product).

references.label: BAT (botulism antitoxin heptavalent) FDA package insert; CDC botulism guidance

poison: Infant botulism (toxin types A and B)
antidote: Human botulism immune globulin IV (BIG-IV, BabyBIG)
mechanism: Human-derived antibodies neutralise circulating botulinum toxin types A and B in infants; reduces duration of hospitalisation and mechanical ventilation. Preferred over equine antitoxin in infants for types A/B.
dosing: Single IV infusion per protocol as soon as infant botulism is suspected; obtained via the designated infant botulism treatment programme.

references.label: Arnon SS et al. Human botulism immune globulin for infant botulism. NEJM 2006; BabyBIG product information

poison: North American pit viper (rattlesnake, copperhead, cottonmouth) envenomation
antidote: Crotalidae polyvalent immune Fab (e.g. CroFab; or F(ab')2 product)
mechanism: Ovine venom-specific Fab fragments bind and neutralise crotalid venom toxins; the small fragments distribute rapidly into tissue. Short Fab half-life can cause recurrent coagulopathy/thrombocytopenia, requiring maintenance dosing and follow-up.
dosing: Initial control dose then scheduled maintenance doses per product protocol; monitor for recurrent coagulopathy. F(ab')2 products have longer half-life. Doses per label.

references.label: Crotalidae polyvalent immune Fab (ovine) prescribing information; Crotalidae envenomation StatPearls

poison: Severe lipophilic drug toxicity (e.g. TCAs, bupropion, verapamil) with cardiovascular collapse
mechanism: Creates an intravascular lipid phase that sequesters highly lipophilic drugs away from target tissues ('lipid sink/shuttle') and may provide a myocardial energy substrate; reported rescue in cardiac arrest/shock from TCAs, bupropion, and calcium-channel blockers refractory to standard care.
dosing: 20% lipid emulsion bolus ~1.5 mL/kg over 1 minute then infusion ~15 mL/kg/hour, per ASRA/AAGBI LAST-derived protocol; reserve for life-threatening toxicity. Doses per protocol.

references.label: Cave G, Harvey M. IV lipid emulsion as antidote beyond local anaesthetic toxicity: systematic review. Acad Emerg Med 2009

mechanism: Competitive mu-opioid receptor antagonist like naloxone but with higher receptor affinity and a much longer duration of action (~8-12 hours). Long action risks prolonged precipitated withdrawal; expert bodies advise it should not replace naloxone as the first-line antidote.
dosing: Up to ~1-2 mg per label is the maximum clinically useful reversal dose; titrate to ventilation. Naloxone remains preferred first-line. Doses per label/protocol.

references.label: ACMT & AACT Joint Position Statement on nalmefene (2023); nalmefene prescribing information

poison: Excessive/prolonged rocuronium or vecuronium neuromuscular blockade
mechanism: Modified gamma-cyclodextrin that encapsulates aminosteroidal neuromuscular blockers (rocuronium > vecuronium) in a 1:1 complex, lowering free drug at the neuromuscular junction and reversing blockade rapidly, including from profound depth. Does not reverse benzylisoquinolinium agents.
dosing: IV per depth of block (e.g. higher doses for profound/immediate reversal) as per anaesthesia protocol; can rarely cause anaphylaxis. Doses per label.

references.label: Sugammadex prescribing information; OpenAnesthesia reversal of neuromuscular blockade

poison: Recent ingestion of a charcoal-adsorbable toxin (general GI decontamination)
mechanism: Adsorbs many drugs/toxins onto its large surface area within the gut, preventing systemic absorption; greatest benefit within 1 hour of ingestion. Does not bind metals, iron, lithium, alcohols, acids or alkalis, and should not be given routinely.
dosing: Consider only if a potentially toxic, charcoal-adsorbable ingestion occurred within ~1 hour and the airway is protected; adult ~50 g orally. Per AACT/EAPCCT position statement.

references.label: AACT/EAPCCT Position Statement: Single-Dose Activated Charcoal (updated)

poison: Salicylate and other weak-acid poisonings (e.g. some herbicides)
mechanism: Raising urine pH (>=7.5) ionises filtered weak acids ('ion trapping'), preventing their tubular reabsorption and enhancing renal elimination; first-line for moderate salicylate poisoning not meeting dialysis criteria. Monitor potassium (hypokalaemia impairs alkalinisation).
dosing: IV sodium bicarbonate (e.g. 1-2 mEq/kg) then bicarbonate-containing fluids titrated to urine pH 7.5-8.5 with potassium repletion. Doses per AACT/EAPCCT position paper.

references.label: AACT/EAPCCT Position Paper on Urine Alkalinization. J Toxicol Clin Toxicol
